By embedding physical power flow constraints into deep residual networks, this method effectively resolves conventional Jacobian ill-conditioning and ensures high-precision, real-time grid perception. Second, a high-resolution, data-driven carbon emission flow tracking model is formulated to dynamically quantify nodal carbon intensities within lossy networks, successfully deriving analytical Locational Marginal Carbon Emissions (LMCE). Finally, to optimally orchestrate these distributed assets, a multi-spatiotemporal scale collaborative control strategy is developed. This advanced architecture utilizes day-ahead spatial-temporal pricing to proactively balance EV load distributions, coupled seamlessly with an intra-day real-time Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework powered by safe Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for precise vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and PV regulation. Extensive numerical simulations conducted on a modified IEEE 33-bus distribution system rigorously validate the framework's absolute superiority in mitigating voltage violations, drastically reducing active power losses, and minimizing systemic carbon footprints.
source: IEEE/IAS Industrial and Commercial Power System Asia (I&CPS Asia)

title: Lightweight Neural Network-Based Cell Balancing Using Variable Effective Resistance
abstract: Cell imbalance can force a series battery pack to stop charging before all cells reach their usable capacity. This paper improves passive balancing without adding a power converter or a selectable resistor bank. Each cell retains one fixed bleed resistor, and pulse-width modulation (PWM) changes its time-averaged effective resistance. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP) uses the five-cell state-of-charge vector to coordinate the duty commands. Conventional logic independently enforces charging, measurement, duty, and temperature limits. The network is trained across the normalized state-of-charge range from 0 to 1 and executes with a fixed computational cost. In a common five-cell NCM simulation, the proposed scheduler reduced the final mean absolute state-of-charge deviation from 0.49 to 0.04 percentage points and reduced balancing time by 36.6% relative to the implemented rule controller, whose hard activation dead-band accounts for a substantial part of the final-deviation gap. Balancing time remained comparable to that of the linear model predictive control reference across a two-decade sweep of its regularization weight, while the proposed scheduler required only fixed-cost inference rather than an online quadratic-program solve. Separately, an Arm Cortex-M4 microcontroller prototype using the original narrower-domain network verified end-to-end operation of the sensing, state estimation, neural inference, constraint enforcement, and PWM actuation path, while the retrained full-domain network was evaluated in simulation. The proposed method therefore provides a practical software upgrade for passive balancers by improving pack-wide duty allocation while retaining the simple resistor–switch circuit.

title: Hierarchical Short-Horizon Model Predictive Control With User Adaptation for Microcontroller-Based Balcony Photovoltaic Energy Management
abstract: Energy management in balcony photovoltaic (PV) systems is becoming increasingly complex with the integration of energy storage, flexible loads, and dynamic electricity prices under time-varying, user-dependent generation and demand. Model predictive control (MPC) can coordinate these flexibilities using forecast information while accounting for system dynamics and operational constraints. However, its computational requirements, particularly with increasing prediction horizons, are relevant for low-cost embedded hardware. This work investigates how an energy management system (EMS) can provide predictive operation under limited computational resources. The examined balcony PV system combines direct-current (DC) and alternating-current (AC) battery storage with thermal energy storage and is evaluated using two residential datasets. Alternative objective formulations, quadratic programming (QP) and mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) structures, and prediction horizons from one to four hours are analyzed. The resulting MPC is extended with replay-based user adaptation to account for individual preferences and enable on-device adaptation. Furthermore, a supervisory strategy incorporates remaining-day forecasts to complement the limited MPC prediction horizon. Results indicate that a two-hour multi-objective QP achieves performance close to the corresponding MILP while avoiding binary decision variables to facilitate embedded implementation. Preference adaptation improves the profile-specific evaluation score in 26 of 32 independent contexts while preserving the dominant user priorities. In extended closed-loop evaluations, strategic supervision reduces PV curtailment by 61.9 % and grid import by 8.8 %, while increasing PV self-consumption by 13.9 and self-sufficiency by 7.0 percentage points. The resulting QP-based controller was successfully implemented and executed on an ESP32-S3, demonstrating feasibility for resource-constrained embedded operation.

title: Next-Generation Transformer and Power Conversion Architectures for Energy-Aware, High-Performance Distribution Networks
abstract: The general trend of increasing integration of the distributed energy resources (DERs), such as solar photovoltaics, wind generation, and electric vehicles (EVs), has turned the distribution networks into dynamic and more complex systems. Fundamental transformer and power conversion designs modeled and optimized as centralized system solutions optimized to support unidirectional power flow are ill suited to supporting the efficiency, reliability and resilience requirements under these changing environments. Specifically, line-frequency transformers and older converters are also limited by their ability to handle transients, such as voltage regulation, breaker and fault tolerance, as well as facilitation of renewable intermittency. The present paper offers the concept of the next-generation distribution network system built on the basis of solid-state transformers (SSTs), modular multilevel converters (MMCs), and bidirectional power electronic interfaces to provide high-performance, energy-aware operation. State-of-the-art control technologies-such as model predictive control (MPC) to enable modal adaptive control, digital twin-based predictive monitoring to enable real-time anomaly detection, and machine learning-driven optimization to empower demand-side management, are incorporated into the proposed architecture. The framework is assessed in a two-stage validation pattern. Technical benefits of simulation studies are quantified by use of IEEE-33 bus radial distribution test system. The results of the paper show that SST-based networks would decrease power losses by 18% and enhance the uniformity of the voltage profile by 10%, and the renewable integration efficiency would be at least 93% in situations of high penetration of DER and EV. Second, embedded systems are practically realizable in HIL validation, using a dSPACE real-time platform, with fault recovery within 3 ms and total harmonic distortion (THD) less than 3% which is in accordance with IEEE 519 standards. The results prove that the combination of SSTs and modular power conversion and smart control of the distribution network helps much to increase the efficiency, resilience, and adaptability, of the distribution networks. Bringing together high-performance power electronics and smart monitoring and optimization open up a scalable path to sustainable, dependable and energy-wise next-generation distribution systems proposed architectures.
source: National Journal of Electrical Machines & Power Conversion

title: Design of an Adaptive Stair-Climbing Robot Based on Heterogeneous Dual-Core Intelligent Control Technology
abstract: With the deepening trend of societal aging, the demand for mobile robots in scenarios such as elderly assistance, disability aid, logistics, and rescue is growing. Navigating stairs in complex, unstructured environments has become a key challenge in robotics. Traditional wheeled, tracked, or legged robots suffer from weak adaptability, insufficient stability, or high cost. This paper designs an adaptive stair-climbing robot utilizing a heterogeneous dual-core control architecture built with an STM32H743 microcontroller and a Raspberry Pi 4B. It integrates multiple sensors including an RGB-D camera, an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU), and encoders. The Raspberry Pi 4B serves as the upper-layer intelligent decision-making core, performing planning and decision-making through fuzzy logic and Model Predictive Control (MPC). The STM32H743 acts as the lower-layer real-time control core, achieving precise execution via PID control. The robot can adapt to stairs with slopes of 30°–45° and step heights of 150–200 mm made of different materials, maintaining a stability margin of no less than 20 mm during climbing. Compared to traditional tracked robots, the stability margin is improved by over 35%. The robot demonstrates good stability and robustness in various stair environments, providing an innovative technical approach for mobile robots in complex terrains.
source: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications

title: MPC-Guided Policy Learning for Real-Time Integrated Longitudinal–Lateral–Vertical Vehicle Motion Control
abstract: Distributed electric vehicles not only offer expanded control authority and performance boundaries but also introduce significant challenges due to strong nonlinear coupling and high-dimensional decision spaces. This article proposes an integrated longitudinal–lateral–vertical vehicle motion control framework that simultaneously addresses multiactuator coordination and real-time computational constraints. A hierarchical architecture is adopted, with an upper level nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) coordinating multiple chassis actuators under coupled dynamics and tire adhesion constraints, and two lower level quadratic programming modules ensuring actuator-level feasibility. To enable real-time execution of the high-dimensional NMPC, an MPC-guided policy learning is developed by incorporating the NMPC objective, dynamics, and constraint information into neural policy learning and training it in a label-free, physics-aware manner via differentiable rollout. Extensive cosimulation demonstrates that the proposed algorithm maintains control performance comparable to that of a CasADi-based NMPC under the evaluated scenarios, while reducing the average computation time by more than two orders of magnitude. Hardware-in-the-loop experiments on an automotive-grade Infineon AURIX TC397 microcontroller ($\approx$US$40) confirm real-time feasibility, with the worst case computation time of only 8.09 ms. Real-vehicle experiments further validate the practical effectiveness of the proposed method under real driving conditions. This highlights the strong potential for on-board deployment.

title: PMBLDCM Based Speed Regulation and Energy Renewal Analysis in Rotating Appliances using MPC and MRAC Strategies
abstract: Permanent Magnet Brushless DC Machine (PMBLDCM), because of its portable size, easy care operation, good efficacy, and high mechanical characteristics, offers better control of rotational speed. Since it provides a more accurate way to control speed, predominantly in rotating fan applications, primarily to improve energy efficiency, ambient comfort, and low aeroacoustics. In the manuscript, PMBLDCM modelling and various control approaches, namely Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Model Reference Adaptive Control (MRAC), are used for performance comparison. The entire drive system is modelled in a closed loop in the MATLAB/SIMULINK platform to examine various parameters, such as speed, Back EMF, and energy renewal, and to determine the best robust control strategy for operation. The speed regulation is practically prototyped using a PIC Microcontroller to generate trigger signals in sequence to improve actuation of the PMBLDCM Drive system.
source: IEEE International Conference on Renewable Energy and Sustainable E-Mobility (RESEM)

title: ENACT: Ensemble Neural Fields for Reactive Robot Control
abstract: Tracking moving targets through clutter and occlusions demands real-time sensorimotor control that adapts to dynamic uncertainty. Model predictive control (MPC) incurs high computational cost, while reinforcement learning requires task-specific retraining. We introduce ENACT (Ensemble Neural Attractor Components for Tracking), a modular framework decomposing reactive control into coordinated Dynamic Neural Fields (DNFs). Each DNF module—attention, gating, memory, context—addresses a distinct sensorimotor primitive through continuous attractor dynamics, enabling runtime reconfiguration without retraining. We benchmark ENACT on both simulation and a Cortex-M7 microcontroller, showing up to 86% lower tracking RMS error, ~2.8× faster disturbance-recovery times, predictable sub-millisecond control latency, and ~9× lower SRAM footprint compared to MPC baseline.

title: A Computationally Efficient Alternative To MPC For Real-Time Torque Vectoring In 4WID EVs
abstract: Four-Wheel Independent Drive (4WID) electric vehicles offer unprecedented authority over individual wheel forces, enabling propulsion-based yaw stability control through torque vectoring. Model Predictive Control (MPC) has emerged as the dominant academic paradigm for multi-objective vehicle dynamic control owing to its constraint-handling capability and predictive horizon structure. However, the online solution of constrained quadratic programs incurs O(n³) computational complexity with respect to the prediction horizon length, rendering real-time deployment on standard automotive embedded controllers impractical for most production-grade applications. This paper proposes an architecture comprising a Sliding Mode Control (SMC) yaw stability controller integrated with a two-dimensional (2D) motor efficiency map (η-map) based torque allocator that resolves the corrective wheel torque distribution problem in O(1) time via direct memory lookup. The SMC formulates a sliding surface combining yaw rate error and sideslip angle error, deploying a boundary-layer saturation function to eliminate chattering while preserving robust stability margins under nonlinear tire dynamics and variable road friction. The efficiency-aware torque allocator pre-computes optimal torque-speed operating regions offline and retrieves them via a 2D lookup table at each control step, achieving multi-objective performance simultaneous stability enhancement and energy efficiency improvementwithout requiring any online optimization. Comparative MATLAB/Simulink evaluation under a standardized step-steer maneuver at 60 km/h on a dry surface (μ = 0.85) demonstrates that the proposed SMC reduces yaw rate root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 51.2% relative to the proportional (P) baseline, by 33.5% relative to PID, and by 37.6% relative to the Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR), while consuming only 139.8 kJ compared to the highest-consumption controller at 142.7 kJ. Theoretical execution time analysis confirms that the proposed architecture is compatible with 1 ms embedded controller cycle times on standard 32-bit automotive-grade microcontrollers, a target that MPC-based alternatives cannot reliably meet without dedicated co-processor hardware.\\n\\n
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: PENGEMBANGAN MODEL PREDICTIVE CONTROL UNTUK ALAT PENGELOS BENANG KAIN TAJUNG BERBASIS INTERNET OF THINGS
abstract: The traditional thread-winding process for Palembang Tajung fabric still relies on manual operation, which may result in inconsistencies in winding speed and thread tension. This study aims to develop a prototype thread-winding machine based on the Internet of Things (IoT) that integrates the Model Predictive Control (MPC) method. The prototype uses an ESP32 microcontroller, an FC-03 optical sensor for rotational-speed measurement, a motor actuator, and the Blynk platform for remote monitoring. Testing involved rotational-speed measurements at 10 target thread lengths ranging from 50 to 500 cm, IoT communication-delay measurements at five observation times, and observations of wound thread length over time. The results show that the rotational-speed measurement errors listed in the table range from 0 to 0.49%. Meanwhile, according to the results table, IoT communication delays range from 0.8 to 2.2 seconds for uplink and from 1.1 to 2.4 seconds for downlink. The recorded wound thread lengths were 3, 8, 22, 30, 56, and 120 cm at observation times of 1, 5, 15, 30, 60, and 150 minutes, respectively. These results indicate that the prototype can perform rotational-speed measurements and support IoT-based monitoring. However, the available experimental data are insufficient to establish the effectiveness of MPC in maintaining stable thread tension or to demonstrate an increase in production speed compared with conventional methods. Therefore, further testing involving direct thread-tension measurements and performance comparisons with conventional thread-winding methods is required.

title: Empirical evaluation of dynamic event-triggered neuro-MPC for MAV attitude control on edge hardware
abstract: Model Predictive Control provides robust attitude control for Micro Aerial Vehicles but demands prohibitive online computing power, hindering its deployment on resource-constrained edge hardware. To resolve this bottleneck, this paper proposes a Dynamic Event-Triggered Neuro-MPC architecture. Offline, a Sobolev-regularized neural network is trained to accurately approximate the expert MPC policy. For edge inference, a dynamic event-triggered mechanism—integrating quadratic error forms and exponential decay—is designed to minimize computational load while ensuring Lyapunov asymptotic stability. Hardware-in-the-loop simulations with Gaussian sensor noise demonstrate that DET-Neuro-MPC eliminates limit cycle oscillations and achieves zero steady-state error tracking, matching the performance of costly online MPC. Crucially, it reduces the edge microcontroller's computational wake-up rate by 78.7%, providing a highly efficient framework for deploying complex control algorithms in aerospace embedded systems.
source: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Smart Manufacturing

title: Isolated Multi-Input Multi-Output Power Supply for Data Centers
abstract: This paper proposes an inverse model predictive control (IMPC) strategy for a six-port multi-active bridge (MAB) converter serving as an isolated multi-input multi-output (MIMO) power supply for data center applications. The proposed control approach simultaneously regulates the DC-link voltages across four dynamic output ports through optimal phase-shift modulation. Moreover, coupling-effect mitigation technique is introduced to estimate and compensate for inter-port interactions in real time. This decouples the voltage regulation process of each output port and enhances the dynamic response of the entire system. The controller is implemented on a lab-scale testbed, and a low-cost microcontroller is adopted to implement the proposed control system. The proposed method is then experimentally verified through a set of tests under different operating conditions.
source: Asia-Pacific Power and Energy Engineering Conference (APPEEC)

title: Edge AI Imitation of Event-Triggered Model Predictive Control for an Inverted Pendulum
abstract: Event-triggered model predictive control (MPC) updates the control input only when needed, but it still solves an optimization problem at every event, which on the studied cart–pole can exceed its 10 ms control period. We propose a compact multi-task neural network that replaces the whole scheme: it decides when to update the input and which value to apply, using only online measurements. It is trained on 500 physical recordings, adapted to a simulated teacher and refined with DAgger. Feeding it the held input produces a copycat policy that is accurate in open loop but sluggish in closed loop; in a matched comparison over four training seeds, removing that input raises full-episode success from three to 39 of 40 episodes. In simulation, at the default sensor noise, the final network completes all swing-up and tracking episodes, with time to upright and tracking error close to the teacher’s, whereas on the simulated teacher, tree ensembles have 1.4–1.6 times its open-loop error. In an open-loop replay on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, a step takes under 40% of the period. In tracking and full episodes, it updates the input 33–39% more often than the teacher, mainly because it does not learn the rule’s sparsity.

title: Nonlinear Model Predictive Control via Behavioral Cloning: Framework, Design and Simulation Assessment
abstract: Over the past decades, there has been significant interest from industries and academics in model predictive control (MPC) due to its capability to systematically handle constraints and nonlinearities during the control process. However, the computational complexity limits real-time deployment, particularly in embedded systems. This paper presents a framework for imitation learning via behavioral cloning to approximate nonlinear MPC (NMPC) policies with significantly reduced computational cost while maintaining expert-level performance. The proposed framework trains a multi-layer perceptron neural network (MLP) to replicate NMPC-based control behavior, effectively reducing approximation errors introduced during training. The resulting framework is then applied to two applications: i) An NMPC-based path following controller (PF) for a scaled robotic vehicle; and ii) An NMPC-based traction controller (TC) for a rear-wheel-drive electric vehicle driving on an icy surface. Simulation results demonstrate that the trained MLP successfully replicates NMPC performance, offering a computationally efficient alternative for real-time applications.

title: Sensitivity-based multistep MPC for embedded systems
abstract: In model predictive control (MPC), an optimization problem is solved every sampling instant to determine an optimal control for a physical system. We aim to accelerate this procedure for fast systems applications and address the challenge of implementing the resulting MPC scheme on an embedded system with limited computing power. We present the sensitivity-based multistep MPC, a strategy which considerably reduces the computing requirements in terms of floating point operations (FLOPs), compared to a standard MPC formulation, while fulfilling closed- loop performance expectations. We illustrate by applying the method to a DC-DC converter model and show how a designer can optimally trade off closed-loop performance considerations with computing requirements in order to fit the controller into a resource-constrained embedded system.
